resources.string: How the small intestine absorbs nutrients
A schematic of normal human absorption. The villus and enlarged cell are not to scale, and the paths show direction, not timing or amounts.
A villus projects into the lumen
Villi increase the surface available for absorption. Each villus is lined with epithelium and contains blood capillaries and a small lymphatic vessel called a lacteal.
An enterocyte is one absorptive cell in the lining of a villus. Tiny microvilli on its lumen-facing surface form the brush border and add still more surface area.
Glucose and amino acids cross enterocytes, leave on the tissue side and enter nearby blood capillaries. Portal blood carries them toward the liver.
After long-chain fat digestion products enter the cell, the enterocyte rebuilds triglycerides and packages them with other lipids and proteins into chylomicrons.
Chylomicrons leave the tissue-facing side of enterocytes and enter the lacteal. Lymph carries them to the bloodstream later, unlike the direct capillary route for glucose and amino acids.
